title: From Dal-Chawal to Policy Blueprint: How Traditional Indian Food Is Shaping America's War on Ultra-Processed Diets
excerpt: A senior adviser to Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has singled out India's centuries-old culinary traditions as a model for the Make America Healthy Again campaign — just as India's own Economic Survey warns the country is losing its food heritage to packaged snacks
body:
When Calley Means, the senior food and nutrition adviser to US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., was asked what country's dietary traditions best illustrate the path away from ultra-processed foods, he did not hesitate. "Each nation has its own culinary heritage," Means told a gathering of Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health fellows, "and there are numerous ways to achieve good health. The key is to value food more, depend less on processed items, and concentrate on nutritional fundamentals like sufficient protein, fibre, and whole foods." The tradition he kept returning to was India's.

The endorsement came during a virtual discussion organised as part of the Health Coverage Fellowship at Harvard, in response to a question from *The Indian Express*. Means — a key architect of the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) initiative — pointed to India's historical emphasis on home-cooked meals, fresh ingredients, intermittent fasting, and mindful eating as a "compelling alternative" to the processed diets now dominant across the developed world. "Exploring what has been effective in India over centuries could be a productive approach," he said. "We must revisit the types of foods and lifestyles that have historically supported human well-being."

## A Validation Long Overdue

For millions of Indians living abroad, the moment carries a particular resonance. NRIs who grew up defending their tiffin boxes and explaining why their mothers packed rotis instead of sandwiches are now watching the US government's most prominent health campaign cite exactly those traditions as a model. The dal-chawal, the fresh sabzi, the yoghurt-with-every-meal rhythm of an Indian household — these were never just comfort food. They were, as Means's framing now suggests, a public health blueprint.

The MAHA campaign has made ultra-processed foods its primary target. Kennedy's Department of Health and Human Services announced plans for a federal definition of ultra-processed foods by April 2026, with front-of-package labelling requirements and updates to school nutrition programmes and SNAP benefits to follow. The movement has drawn both praise and scepticism — food industry groups have pushed back aggressively, and Kennedy himself faced criticism for endorsing a meals company whose products contained the very additives he campaigns against — but its core thesis is straightforward: Americans eat too much food that is industrially manufactured and too little food that is real.

## India's Own Paradox

The irony, however, is sharp. Even as American policymakers look to Indian food culture for inspiration, India itself is rapidly abandoning it. The Economic Survey 2025-26, tabled before Parliament earlier this year, flagged ultra-processed foods as a key driver of India's obesity crisis. The numbers are stark: retail UPF sales in India jumped from $0.9 billion in 2006 to roughly $38 billion by 2019 — a near 40-fold increase. Sales expanded by over 150 per cent between 2009 and 2023. Nearly one in four Indian adults is now obese, and childhood obesity is projected to surge from 3.3 crore in 2020 to 8.3 crore by 2035 if current trends continue.

A separate study found that UPF consumption in North India is nearly twice that of South India, driven by income, urbanisation, and the aggressive marketing of packaged snacks and sweetened beverages. The WHO has published detailed analysis of India's UPF market expansion, calling for policy intervention to promote traditional diets and indigenous cooking practices — a recommendation India's own Economic Survey echoes.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs, the story has a dual edge. On one hand, there is a quiet vindication in seeing the food culture they carried across oceans recognised at the highest levels of American health policy. The emphasis on home-cooking, seasonal eating, and the use of turmeric, ghee, fermented foods, and legumes — staples that were once dismissed as exotic or unhealthy by Western nutritionists — is now being reframed as precisely what modern diets lack.

On the other, there is the disquieting awareness that the India they left behind is moving in the opposite direction. The next generation in Delhi, Mumbai, and Bengaluru is growing up on Maggi, packaged juices, and delivery-app meals. The very traditions that Means holds up as a model are under siege in the country that produced them.

Means's prescription for urban children, including those in India, was blunt: increase real food intake, reduce ultra-processed items, enhance physical activity, improve sleep quality, and cultivate healthy habits from an early age. "Ultimately, our message is that maintaining health is simpler than many people perceive," he said. "People used to be naturally active throughout their daily routines. There were no gyms or structured fitness programmes; daily life was inherently more physically engaging."

## What's Next

The MAHA campaign's direction will be tested in the coming months as the federal UPF definition takes shape and industry lobbying intensifies. For India, the Economic Survey's warning may mark the beginning of a more serious policy conversation about protecting traditional food systems. For NRIs caught between both worlds, the message is both simple and urgent: the food your grandmother made was not just love. It was medicine. And both countries need it back.
